newsitem.title: POLAND: OPINION - Stanislaw Gomulka on Polish budget plan.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Stanislaw Gomulka on Polish budget plan.

text.p: By Stanislaw Gomulka, professor at the London School of Economics and advisor to the National Bank of Poland.

In 1997, the deficit of the central government is expected to be 2.8 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), and the general government deficit to be 3.0 percent. This compares with 2.8 percent this year, 2.6 percent in 1995 and 2.5 percent in 1994.

This upward trend is contrary to the government's Strategy for Poland 1994, which called for a gradual reduction in the deficit to two percent of GDP in 1997. Although the planned 1997 deficit is only marginally worse than the expected outcome this year, it falls short of what is needed to sustain growth and disinflation in the medium term.
BUDGET CURRENT ACCOUNT, TRADE PREDICTIONS TOO OPTIMISTIC
The main short-term problem in the budget is the contradiction between targets concerning trade and current account balances and planned monetary and fiscal policies.

If we keep the end-1997 inflation target of 13 percent, the planned credit expansion by the government, households and the corporate sector is likely to translate into much wider trade and current account deficits than the budget assumes and possibly a significant drop in foreign reserves.
The $3.9 billion current account deficit assumed in the 1997 draft budget seems much too optimistic. The deficit will probably reach about $8 billion, or five to six percent of GDP.
Since March 1996 exports have stayed roughly flat and the budget assumption of a 15 percent increase in 1997 on a year-to-year basis now seems quite unrealistic.
Imports continue to expand at an annual rate of about 30 percent, fuelled mainly by rising incomes and credit.
CREDIT EXPANSION TO TRIGGER HIGHER MARKET RATES
The 1997 draft budget assumes that credit for households and companies will grow by about 10 percent in real terms and 25 percent nominally.
Strong credit expansion has been a significant factor behind the extremely fast widening of the trade deficit this year, and the trend is likely to continue next year.

The inflation target seems more or less realistic, especially as much higher bank financing of public spending, combined with a likely fall in foreign reserves, will likely lead to higher both real and nominal interest rates.
The registered trade deficit could well exceed the $9.5 billion assumed in the draft budget, reaching possibly as much as $13-14 billion.

This sharp deterioration will coincide with a moderate decline in the surplus in unregistered cross-border trade, pushing the current account deficit to about $7 billion. The deficit is unlikely to be offset fully by the inflow of foreign capital.
A LIKELY DROP IN RESERVES TO TIGHTEN MONEY SUPPLY

Consequently, foreign reserves may fall by as much as $2-3 billion, reducing by some six to seven billion zlotys or four percent the targeted money supply and thus exerting strong upward pressure on market interest rates.

The National Bank of Poland (NBP) has announced its wish to have bigger exchange rate fluctuations within the 14-percent trading band but, together with the government, is against letting the crawling devaluation exceed the planned nine percent, this in order to protect the inflation target.
The fall in foreign currency reserves would not materialise if portfolio investments were to exceed substantially the $1.5 billion forecast in the draft budget, but I would not expect this to happen.
Portfolio investors react positively to expectations of an appreciation of the real effective exchange rate, but in 1997 a devaluation rather than an appreciation may be anticipated.

This kind of expectation gives the NBP greater scope for manoeuvre, as it can accept a relatively large increase in real market interest rates without fears that higher rates will prompt a strong influx of short-term capital from abroad.
The central bank and the government may nevertheless face the dilemma of ranking their key macroeconomic objectives, once it becomes apparent that they cannot achieve them all simultaneously.
If they stick to the inflation target of 13 percent, there will probably be either a considerable worsening of the balance of payments or a somewhat lower rate of economic growth.
In the latter case, there would be greater pressure on the budget due to a higher cost of servicing the public debt (because interest rates will be higher) and because of lower tax revenues.
SLIGHT OVERSHOOT OF INFLATION, C/A AND GROWTH TARGETS SEEN
Currency reserves are sufficiently high for a fall of even $2-3 billion in one year to be acceptable. But it would be bad if such a decline were to be repeated in subsequent years.
It therefore appears that the budget apart, a certain increase in real interest rates is needed anyway, as growth in non-government credit is clearly excessive.
The NBP's actions in this direction would weaken the tendency towards worsening the balance of payments.
Neverthless, a very large increase in real market interest rates may not be acceptable, even if actions to restrain these rates were to cause somewhat higher than planned inflation.

I therefore expect that this potential conflict, if it arises, between the three basic objectives concerning inflation, economic growth and the balance of payments, will be resolved by missing somewhat all the objectives rather than by placing the entire burden of underachievement on any single objective.
In 1997 the planned progress in reducing inflation is achievable mainly because it will be possible to allow foreign reserves to stabilise or even to fall.

As this fall of reserves cannot be allowed in 1998 and subsequent years, bearing in mind the necessity to reduce inflation to Western European levels, it will be necessary to again limit bank credit to the government.

Therefore we return to the question of a reform of public finance. Here the solution is well known -- a social security reform, limits on social spending in relation to GDP, larger revenues from privatisation, a reduction of subsidies to enterprises and lowering the cost of servicing the public debt.
